\chapter{Four Verbs of the Mind}
\label{ch:ta-verbs-of-the-mind}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I think, I understand, I read and I write in Tamil with the same three slots, tell a strong verb from a weak one by its held consonant, explain why \ta{எனக்குப்} \ta{புரிகிறது} has no I in it, and make the \ta{ழ} in \ta{எழுது}.}

Say \ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{எழுதுகிறேன்}, run the chapter's four verbs in the present and sort them into strong and weak, produce \ta{ழ} without letting the tongue touch, and name the one word here whose origin is unsettled.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ninai]{\ta{நினை} (ninai) — \textquotedblleft{}to think,\textquotedblright{} which is also \textquotedblleft{}to remember\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C33-ninai}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Teri} refused to carry a person: \emph{enakku teriyum}, \textquotedblleft{}it is known to me.\textquotedblright{} Say \emph{enakkut tamiḻ teriyum} once. This verb takes the person back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நினை}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நினை}} — \emph{ninai} — \textbf{to think; to think of, to remember}
\end{quote}

Two light beats, \emph{ni-nai}. Threaded up: \textbf{\ta{நினைக்கிறேன்}} (\emph{ninaikkiṟēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{} — stem, tense, person, with nothing new in the machine.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ta{நி}} is the \textbf{dental \ta{ந}} with the \emph{i} sign \textbf{\ta{ி}}; \textbf{\ta{னை}} is the \textbf{alveolar \ta{ன}} with the \emph{ai} sign \textbf{\ta{ை}}. Two of Tamil's three n-letters in one word, and not interchangeable: the first sits on the teeth, the second on the ridge behind them. Chapter 6's three-n lesson mapped all three — \textbf{\ta{ந}}, \textbf{\ta{ன}}, \textbf{\ta{ண}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it doubles, so it is strong}]
The \textbf{k} in \emph{ninaikkiṟēṉ} is held long — \emph{ninaik-ki} — as it was in \emph{irukkiṟēṉ} and \emph{pārkkiṟēṉ}, and not as it was in \emph{pōgiṟēṉ}. So \textbf{\ta{நினை} is strong}, and its past is \textbf{\ta{நினைத்தேன்}} (\emph{ninaittēṉ}), with the strong verb's doubled \emph{t}.

One held consonant answers a question you would otherwise ask of every new verb. You are not learning a machine per verb: you learn which of two camps a stem sits in, then reuse the same three slots forever.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{நினை}} is native Dravidian and does two English jobs at once: \emph{ninaikkiṟēṉ} is \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{} and equally \textquotedblleft{}I remember.\textquotedblright{} The noun says so — \textbf{\ta{நினைவு}} (\emph{ninaivu}) is \textbf{memory}. Kannada agrees with \textbf{\ka{ನೆನೆ}} (\emph{nene}), \textquotedblleft{}remember,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ka{ನೆನಪು}} (\emph{nenapu}), \textquotedblleft{}memory\textquotedblright{}; Malayalam has \textbf{\ml{നിനയ്ക്കുക}} (\emph{ninaykkuka}).

One honest note for this chapter and the next: English took real words from Tamil — \emph{catamaran}, \emph{mango}, \emph{curry}, \emph{pariah} — but \textbf{none from these verbs}. Inventing a cousin would be worse than having none.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ninai\textquotedblright{} — think, remember — then \textquotedblleft{}ninaikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the strong pair — \textquotedblleft{}irukkiṟēṉ … ninaikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the noun — \textquotedblleft{}ninaivu\textquotedblright{}, memory — then Kannada \textquotedblleft{}nenapu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two shapes — \textquotedblleft{}enakku teriyum … nāṉ ninaikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two English verbs does \emph{ninai} cover, and which camp is it in? (\textbf{Think} and \textbf{remember}; \textbf{strong}, from the held \emph{kk}.) What is \emph{ninaivu}, and which sister keeps the root? (\textbf{Memory}; \textbf{Kannada}, \emph{nene} / \emph{nenapu}.) Which two n's does \emph{ninai} use, in order? (\textbf{Dental \ta{ந}}, then \textbf{alveolar \ta{ன}}.) And why does \emph{teriyum} carry no \emph{-ēṉ}? (\textbf{Knowing happens to you} — its person sits in the dative instead.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puri]{\ta{புரி} (puri) — \textquotedblleft{}to become clear,\textquotedblright{} and who it becomes clear to}

\label{lesson:TA-C33-puri}



\begin{quote}
Two shapes. \emph{Nāṉ ninaikkiṟēṉ} — I do the thinking. \emph{Enakku teriyum} — the knowing happens to me. Say both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{புரி}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{புரி}} — \emph{puri} — \textbf{to be understood; to become clear}
\end{quote}

The everyday form is \textbf{\ta{புரிகிறது}} (\emph{purigiṟadu}):

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எனக்குத்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{புரிகிறது}.} — \emph{enakkut tamiḻ purigiṟadu} — \textquotedblleft{}I understand Tamil.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Word for word, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to me} Tamil is becoming clear.\textquotedblright{} The verb is weak: the softened \emph{-giṟ-} of \emph{pōgiṟēṉ}, not the long \emph{-kkiṟ-} of \emph{ninaikkiṟēṉ}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ta{பு}} is \textbf{\ta{ப}} carrying the \emph{u} sign, which fuses into the letter's shape rather than hanging off it; \textbf{\ta{ரி}} is \textbf{\ta{ர}} with the \emph{i} sign \textbf{\ta{ி}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the last slot can say \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}}]
\emph{Teriyum} had no person slot at all. \emph{Purigiṟadu} \textbf{fills} it, with \textbf{-\ta{அது}} (\emph{-adu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it}.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{புரி}} + \textbf{\ta{கிற்}} + \textbf{\ta{அது}} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{புரிகிறது}}
\end{quote}

So the thing becoming clear is \emph{it}, and the understander is pushed out of the verb into the dative word \textbf{\ta{எனக்கு}} (\emph{enakku}) that Chapter 6 built for this job. Change the understander and only that word moves:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{enakku purigiṟadu} — I understand
  \item \emph{uṉakku purigiṟadu} — you understand
  \item \emph{avaṉukku purigiṟadu} — he understands
\end{itemize}

Two verbs, two mechanisms, one result: \textbf{the experiencer sits in the dative.} Not an exception — the ordinary way to report what happens inside a person.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Tamil's dictionaries keep more than one \textbf{\ta{புரி}}: an old literary one, \textquotedblleft{}to do, to perform,\textquotedblright{} and this everyday one. Whether they are one root is \textbf{not settled}. Certain is the verbal noun in \emph{-\ta{தல்}}: \textbf{\ta{புரிதல்}} (\emph{puridal}), \textquotedblleft{}understanding.\textquotedblright{}

The family evidence is stronger. Each sister chose a different verb, and every one puts the understander in the dative:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ನನಗೆ} \ka{ಅರ್ಥವಾಯಿತು}} — \emph{nanage arthavāyitu}
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{అర్థమైంది}} — \emph{nāku arthamaindi}
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മനസ്സിലായി}} — \emph{enikku manassilāyi}, \textquotedblleft{}it entered my mind\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Different words, one grammar. Chapter 6 showed the four dative endings were cousins; here they do the same job in the same sentence.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}enakkut tamiḻ purigiṟadu\textquotedblright{} — I understand Tamil
  \item three understanders, one verb — \textquotedblleft{}enakku … uṉakku … avaṉukku purigiṟadu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that share a shape — \textquotedblleft{}enakku teriyum … enakku purigiṟadu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sisters' datives — \textquotedblleft{}enakku … nanage … nāku … enikku\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{puri} mean underneath \textquotedblleft{}understand,\textquotedblright{} and what fills its person slot? (\textbf{To become clear}; \textbf{-\ta{அது}}, \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}.) So where does the understander go? (\textbf{Into the dative} — \emph{enakku}.) Name the other verb that puts you there. (\emph{\textbf{Teri}} — \emph{enakku teriyum}.) And which verb from this chapter keeps the person on the ending? (\emph{\textbf{Ninai}} — \emph{nāṉ ninaikkiṟēṉ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paḍi]{\ta{படி} (paḍi) — \textquotedblleft{}to read,\textquotedblright{} and the letter that is two sounds}

\label{lesson:TA-C33-padi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{enakkut tamiḻ purigiṟadu} — Tamil becomes clear to me. Now the verb for the work that gets you there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{படி}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{படி}} — \emph{paḍi} — \textbf{to read; to study, to learn}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{படிக்கிறேன்}} (\emph{paḍikkiṟēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I read, I study.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{kk} is held, so \textbf{\ta{படி} is strong}, like \emph{ninai} and \emph{pār}; its past is \textbf{\ta{படித்தேன்}} (\emph{paḍittēṉ}).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{படிக்கிறேன்}.} — \emph{nāṉ tamiḻ paḍikkiṟēṉ} — \textquotedblleft{}I study Tamil.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Tamil does not split reading from studying: \textbf{\ta{படிப்பு}} (\emph{paḍippu}) is both \textquotedblleft{}reading\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}an education.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ta{ப}} (\emph{pa}) + \textbf{\ta{டி}}, which is \textbf{\ta{ட}} wearing the \emph{i} sign \textbf{\ta{ி}}.

Now a mystery worth clearing up. The letter is \textbf{\ta{ட}}, named \emph{ṭa}, yet the word is written here \emph{paḍi}, with a \textbf{d}. Nothing is inconsistent: \textbf{Tamil marks no voicing.} One letter covers both sounds and \textbf{position decides} — hard word-initially or doubled, soft between vowels. That is Chapter 5's rule for \textbf{\ta{க}}, which spells \emph{k}, \emph{g} and a soft \emph{h} without changing shape.

So \textbf{\ta{ட}} is soft between the vowels of \emph{paḍi} and hard in the doubled \textbf{\ta{ட்ட}} of \emph{paḍittēṉ}. It is why \emph{pō} becomes \emph{pōgiṟēṉ}, why \emph{sāppiḍu} has a \emph{ḍ}, and why every romanization here softens where a speaker softens.

\textbf{\ta{ட}} is also \textbf{retroflex}, made where \textbf{\ta{ண}} is: tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth. That curl matters more than the \emph{d}-versus-\emph{t}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Tamil's own dictionaries list \textbf{\ta{படி}} as native. Others connect it to Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{पठ्}} (\emph{paṭh}), \textquotedblleft{}to recite, to read aloud\textquotedblright{} — not a silly idea, because \textbf{Tamil has no aspirated consonants}, so a borrowed \emph{paṭh} would arrive as \emph{paṭi} automatically, with no letter to carry the puff of breath.

Next door the evidence is split. Malayalam says \textbf{\ml{പഠിക്കുക}} (\emph{paṭhikkuka}) and \textbf{keeps the aspirate}, in the Sanskrit-series letter \textbf{\ml{ഠ}}; Kannada and Telugu use \textbf{\ka{ಓದು}} (\emph{ōdu}) and \textbf{\te{చదువు}} (\emph{caduvu}), unrelated to either candidate.

Carry away the certain part: \textbf{an aspirate cannot survive into Tamil}, so a stripped-down look-alike is never by itself proof of borrowing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāṉ tamiḻ paḍikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} — I study Tamil
  \item the soft and the hard \ta{ட} — \textquotedblleft{}paḍi … paḍittēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the strong three — \textquotedblleft{}ninaikkiṟēṉ, paḍikkiṟēṉ, pārkkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the weak one beside them — \textquotedblleft{}purigiṟadu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is \textbf{\ta{ட}} written one way and heard two ways, and where is it made? (\textbf{Tamil marks no voicing} — position decides, as with \textbf{\ta{க}}; and it is \textbf{retroflex}, made where \textbf{\ta{ண}} is.) Is \emph{paḍi} borrowed from Sanskrit \emph{paṭh}, and what can Tamil never keep from a Sanskrit word? (\textbf{Unsettled}; \textbf{the aspiration}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I study Tamil.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nāṉ tamiḻ paḍikkiṟēṉ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tamiḻ]{\ta{தமிழ்} — the letter the language is named for}

\label{lesson:TA-W16-read-tamizh}



\begin{quote}
This book has said more than once that Tamil keeps three \emph{l}-letters, and the strand has shown you two: \textbf{\ta{ல}} in \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}}, \textbf{\ta{ள}} in \textbf{\ta{நீங்கள்}}. The third has been outstanding since chapter 18. Here it is, in the word it matters most in.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{த} and \ta{ழ}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{த}} & \emph{ta} — the dental \emph{t}, tongue on the teeth \\
\textbf{\ta{ழ}} & \emph{ḻ} — the third \emph{l}-letter, curled far back \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ta{த}} is the dental partner of the retroflex \textbf{\ta{ட}} you read in \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}}: same kind of stop, different place in the mouth. Tamil keeps the pair apart in writing, so \textbf{\ta{த}} and \textbf{\ta{ட}} are never interchangeable.

\textbf{\ta{ழ}} is the one Tamil is known for. It is made further back than \textbf{\ta{ள}}, and its sound sits somewhere between an \emph{r}, an \emph{l} and a \emph{zh} — rare enough in the world's languages that Tamil is sometimes called the \textbf{ḻ} language. That is why the word for the language itself ends in it.

\begin{quote}
Read both; do not draw them yet. Neither \textbf{\ta{த}} nor \textbf{\ta{ழ}} has an entry in this book's script data, so neither gets a stroke order, and the mouth positions above are this lesson's own — the data is sourced for \textbf{\ta{ண}}'s retroflex curl and nothing else here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: build the word}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{த}} & \emph{ta} & this lesson \\
\textbf{\ta{மி}} & \emph{mi} — \ta{ம} with the \ta{ி} sign & \ta{ம} from \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}, \ta{ி} from \textbf{\ta{நன்றி}} \\
\textbf{\ta{ழ்}} & bare \emph{ḻ} — \textbf{\ta{ழ}} under a puḷḷi & this lesson \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{த} · \ta{மி} · \ta{ழ்} $\to$ \ta{தமிழ்}}
\end{quote}

Three pieces, and you can now read the name of the language you have been speaking since page one. That was the plan: the word first, the letters when they can be earned.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{த}} · \textbf{\ta{ழ}} — then \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}tamiḻ\textquotedblright{} — and hold that last sound
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ta{த}} and \textbf{\ta{ட}} — dental and retroflex, teeth and roof
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ta{ல}} · \textbf{\ta{ள}} · \textbf{\ta{ழ}} — all three \emph{l}-letters, at last
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}}. Which letter is \textbf{\ta{த}}'s retroflex partner? (\textbf{\ta{ட}}, from \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}}.) Which of the three \emph{l}-letters ends the word, and what is the dot doing? (\textbf{\ta{ழ}}; the puḷḷi \textbf{removes its built-in \emph{a}}.) Next: the verb for writing — spelled with the \ta{ழ} you just met.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eḻudu]{\ta{எழுது} (eḻudu) — \textquotedblleft{}to write,\textquotedblright{} and the sound Tamil is named for}

\label{lesson:TA-C33-ezhutu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ninaikkiṟēṉ}, \emph{purigiṟadu}, \emph{paḍikkiṟēṉ} — think, understand, read. Say all three. The fourth is reading's other half.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{எழுது}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எழுது}} — \emph{eḻudu} — \textbf{to write; to draw}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{எழுதுகிறேன்}} (\emph{eḻudugiṟēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I write.\textquotedblright{} The tense bead is the \textbf{single softened \emph{-giṟ-}}, so \textbf{\ta{எழுது} is weak}, like \emph{pō} and \emph{sāppiḍu}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{எழுதுகிறேன்}.} — \emph{nāṉ tamiḻ eḻudugiṟēṉ} — \textquotedblleft{}I write Tamil.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ta{எ}} is the standing vowel \emph{e}; \textbf{\ta{ழு}} is \textbf{\ta{ழ}} with the \emph{u} sign and \textbf{\ta{து}} is \textbf{\ta{த}} with the same sign.

The dot returns in the noun \textbf{\ta{எழுத்து}} (\emph{eḻuttu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a letter of the alphabet},\textquotedblright{} spelled \textbf{\ta{எ} \ta{ழு} \ta{த்} \ta{து}}: a \textbf{puḷḷi} strips the vowel from the first \textbf{\ta{த்}} and the second \textbf{\ta{து}} stands whole beside it. Two full letters and a visible dot, never a fused shape: the puḷḷi lesson's bargain.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\ta{ழ}} — written \emph{ḻ} — is the sound in \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}} (\emph{tamiḻ}) itself and in \textbf{\ta{வாழ்}} (\emph{vāḻ}), \textquotedblleft{}to live,\textquotedblright{} and is reputed to be the language's hardest.

Curl the tongue tip back as for \textbf{\ta{ட}} or \textbf{\ta{ண}}, then \textbf{do not let it touch}. Leave a gap and voice through it: what comes out sits between an American \emph{r} and an \emph{l}, and it is a \textbf{glide}, not a stop.

Two honest notes. Many fluent speakers merge \textbf{\ta{ழ}} with \textbf{\ta{ள}} and are understood everywhere. And the family already voted — Chapter 7 gave you Tamil \textbf{ēḻu} against Kannada \textbf{ēḷu}. Kannada and Telugu each had a letter for it and let it go; \textbf{Tamil and Malayalam kept it.}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
The Dravidian etymological dictionary files \textbf{\ta{எழுது}} under \textbf{\ta{எழு}} (\emph{eḻu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to rise}\textquotedblright{} — a written line being a mark raised onto a surface. Standard rather than proven, but native, unlike the open question \emph{paḍi} left you with. Beside it sits \textbf{\ta{எழுத்தாளர்}} (\emph{eḻuttāḷar}), a writer.

The cousin is exact: Malayalam \textbf{\ml{എഴുതുക}} (\emph{eḻutuka}), same verb, same \textbf{\ml{ഴ}}. Kannada and Telugu, having dropped the sound, dropped the verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three \ta{ழ} words — \textquotedblleft{}tamiḻ … vāḻ … eḻudu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāṉ tamiḻ eḻudugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} — I write Tamil
  \item the chapter — \textquotedblleft{}ninaikkiṟēṉ, purigiṟadu, paḍikkiṟēṉ, eḻudugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the split — \textquotedblleft{}Tamil ēḻu … Kannada ēḷu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the chapter's four verbs and name the two weak ones. (\emph{Ninaikkiṟēṉ, purigiṟadu, paḍikkiṟēṉ, eḻudugiṟēṉ}; \emph{\textbf{puri}} and \emph{\textbf{eḻudu}}.) How is \textbf{\ta{ழ}} made, and who kept it? (\textbf{Curled back, not touching}; \textbf{Malayalam} did, \textbf{Kannada} and \textbf{Telugu} dropped it.) What keeps the two \textbf{\ta{த}}'s of \emph{eḻuttu} apart, and which word here has an unsettled origin? (\textbf{The puḷḷi}; \emph{\textbf{paḍi}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
